lessons.title: Personal Hygiene for Food Handlers
lessons.body:
As a tomato paste and sauce producer, your hands, clothes, and health directly affect the safety of your product. Customers trust you not to make them sick. Personal hygiene is your first line of defence.

Always wash your hands with soap and clean running water for at least 20 seconds before starting work, after using the toilet, after handling waste, after coughing or sneezing, and after touching animals. Use a nail brush to clean under your fingernails. Dry hands with a clean towel or air dryer. If water is scarce, use a hand sanitiser with at least 60% alcohol after washing. Never wear rings, watches, or bracelets while handling tomatoesâthey trap dirt and bacteria. Keep fingernails short and unpainted. Cover any cuts or sores with a waterproof plaster.

Wear clean protective clothing: an apron, a hairnet or cap, and closed shoes. If you have long hair, tie it back. Change your apron daily or whenever it gets dirty. Do not wear your work clothes outside the processing area. If you are sick with vomiting, diarrhoea, fever, or open wounds on your hands, do not handle food. Stay home or work away from production until you are well. Even a mild illness can spread dangerous germs.

Avoid touching your face, hair, or phone while working. If you must cough or sneeze, turn away and cover your mouth with your elbow, then wash your hands. Do not eat, drink, or smoke in the processing area. Keep a clean set of clothes at work if possible. Train all workers on these rules and post them on the wall in simple language or pictures.

Remember: good hygiene protects your business. One sick customer can ruin your reputation. Make handwashing stations with soap, water, and a bin for waste easily available. Lead by exampleâif you follow the rules, your workers will too.

lessons.title: Cleaning and Sanitising Equipment and Work Surfaces
lessons.body:
Tomato residue left on equipment can grow bacteria, mould, and attract pests. Cleaning removes dirt; sanitising kills germs. You need both.

Start by scraping off solid tomato waste into a bin. Then wash all equipmentâknives, cutting boards, pots, blenders, filling machinesâwith warm water and dish soap. Use a brush to scrub corners and cracks. Rinse with clean water. For sanitising, mix 1 tablespoon of unscented bleach (5% sodium hypochlorite) in 4 litres of clean water. Soak or wipe surfaces with this solution for at least 1 minute. Let air dryâdo not rinse. For stainless steel, you can also use a food-grade sanitiser. Never mix bleach with other chemicals.

Work surfaces like tables and chopping boards must be cleaned and sanitised before and after each use, and every 4 hours during continuous production. If you switch from raw tomatoes to finished sauce, clean in between to avoid cross-contamination. Use colour-coded cutting boards: red for raw tomatoes, green for finished products, if possible.

Clean floors, walls, and drains daily. Remove all waste to a covered bin outside the processing room. Keep cleaning tools like mops and brushes clean and stored off the floor. After cleaning, wash your hands again. Inspect equipment for cracks or damageâbacteria hide there. Replace worn parts.

Make a cleaning schedule: list what to clean, how often, and who does it. Sign off after each task. This keeps everyone accountable. At the end of the day, do a deep clean: dismantle equipment, clean behind machines, and sanitise everything. A clean workplace also motivates workers and shows customers you care.

lessons.title: Safe Water Use in Tomato Processing
lessons.body:
Water is used for washing tomatoes, cleaning equipment, and making sauce. If the water is dirty, your product becomes dangerous. Only use water that is safe to drink (potable water).

If you rely on a well, borehole, or river, test it at least once a year for bacteria like E. coli. If testing is not available, treat water by boiling for 1 minute, or add 2 drops of unscented bleach per litre, stir, and wait 30 minutes. For large volumes, use a ceramic water filter or UV treatment. Store treated water in clean, covered containers. Never use water from a container that held chemicals.

When washing tomatoes, use clean running water. Do not soak them in a basin of dirty waterâthat spreads dirt. If water is scarce, use a three-basin system: first basin for rinsing off soil, second with soap, third with clean water for final rinse. Change water frequentlyâat least every 30 minutes or when it looks dirty. For the final rinse, use water with 1 teaspoon of bleach per 4 litres to kill germs.

Water used for cleaning surfaces and equipment must also be potable. Do not use greywater or rainwater without treatment. If you use ice, make it from potable water only. Steam used for heating sauce must come from clean water.

After processing, dispose of wastewater properlyâdo not let it pool near the processing area, as it breeds mosquitoes and bacteria. Train workers to never drink from the same cup or use dirty containers. Keep a dedicated tap for handwashing with soap. Safe water is not expensive if you plan: boil, filter, or chlorinate. Your customersâ health depends on it.

lessons.title: Preventing Contamination from Pests and Animals
lessons.body:
Pests like rats, cockroaches, flies, and ants carry dangerous germs. Animalsâdogs, cats, chickensâcan also contaminate your tomatoes and equipment. Keep them out.

Start with proofing your building: seal cracks in walls and floors, fix holes in screens, and install door sweeps. Keep doors and windows closed or screened. Use wire mesh with holes no larger than 6 mm. Store all food and waste in sealed containers. Do not leave dirty dishes or tomato waste overnight. Clean up spills immediately.

Set traps and baits for rats and cockroaches, but place them away from food areas. Use fly traps or ultraviolet light traps. Never use rat poison inside the processing roomâit can contaminate food. If you see pests, act fast: call a professional pest control service. Keep a log of pest sightings and actions taken.

Do not allow animals inside the processing area. If you keep livestock, fence them away from the building. Keep pets out. If you have a cat for rodent control, keep it out of production rooms and provide a separate feeding area. Bird droppings on roofs can wash into water tanksâcover tanks tightly.

Maintain a clean outside area: cut grass short, remove rubbish, and clear stagnant water. Pests hide in clutter. Store firewood and equipment away from walls. Inspect incoming tomatoes for pests or damageâreject rotten ones. After any pest activity, clean and sanitise the affected area thoroughly. Train workers to report signs of pests immediately. A pest-free facility protects your product and your reputation.

lessons.title: Safe Storage of Raw and Finished Products
lessons.body:
Proper storage keeps tomatoes and finished sauce safe from spoilage and contamination. Raw tomatoes should be stored in clean, dry crates off the floor on pallets. Keep them in a cool, shaded areaâideal temperature is 10â15Â°C. Do not stack them too high to avoid bruising. Use within 2â3 days. Never store tomatoes with chemicals, cleaning agents, or raw meat.

Finished tomato paste and sauce must be stored in clean, sealed containers. Glass jars or food-grade plastic bottles work well. After filling, seal immediately. For long shelf life, pasteurise or add acid (like lemon juice or vinegar) to lower pH below 4.6. Store in a cool, dark placeâbelow 25Â°C. Once opened, keep in the refrigerator and use within 5 days. Label with production date and batch number.

Keep raw and finished products separate to avoid cross-contamination. Use separate storage areas or shelves: raw tomatoes on bottom shelves, finished products on top. Never store finished sauce in containers that held raw tomatoes without washing and sanitising first. Use the FIFO rule: First In, First Outâsell older stock first.

Check stored products daily for spoilage: look for mould, gas bubbles, off-smells, or leaking seals. Discard any suspect product immediately. Keep storage areas clean, dry, and pest-free. Do not store products directly on the floorâuse pallets or shelves at least 15 cm off the ground. Maintain a temperature log if you have a refrigerator. Train workers on proper stacking and rotation. Good storage reduces waste and keeps customers safe.

lessons.title: Understanding Common Foodborne Illnesses and How to Avoid Them
lessons.body:
Foodborne illnesses come from harmful bacteria, viruses, or parasites in food. Common ones in tomato products include Salmonella, E. coli, Listeria, and mould toxins. Symptoms include stomach cramps, diarrhoea, vomiting, fever, and sometimes death, especially in children, elderly, and sick people.

Salmonella often comes from dirty hands, unclean equipment, or animal waste. E. coli comes from contaminated water or raw manure. Listeria can grow in cold, wet environments like refrigerators. Moulds produce mycotoxins, which are dangerous even if you scrape off the mould. To avoid these, follow strict hygiene: wash hands, clean equipment, use safe water, and keep pests out.

Prevent cross-contamination: never let raw tomatoes touch finished sauce. Use separate cutting boards and utensils. Cook or pasteurise sauce to at least 85Â°C for 15 minutes to kill bacteria. Acidify with lemon juice or vinegar to pH below 4.6âthis stops bacterial growth. Store food below 5Â°C or above 60Â°C; bacteria grow fastest between 5Â°C and 60Â°C.

If you or a worker has diarrhoea or vomiting, do not handle food. After using the toilet, wash hands thoroughly. Keep a clean toilet with soap and water. Dispose of waste properly. Train everyone on the signs of illness and the importance of reporting sickness. If a customer complains of illness after eating your product, investigate immediately: check your records, clean everything, and if needed, recall the batch.

Remember: prevention is cheaper than treatment. A single outbreak can close your business. Follow the rules every dayâno shortcuts. Your customersâ health and your livelihood depend on it.

quiz.q: How long should you wash your hands with soap and water?
quiz.explanation: 20 seconds is the minimum recommended time to effectively remove germs.

quiz.q: Which of these should you NOT wear while handling tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: Jewellery traps dirt and bacteria and can fall into food.

quiz.q: If you have diarrhoea, what should you do?
options: B) Stay away from food handling
quiz.explanation: Diarrhoea can spread dangerous germs; you must not handle food until well.

quiz.q: What is the correct order for cleaning equipment?
quiz.explanation: Cleaning removes dirt first, then sanitising kills germs.

quiz.q: How much bleach should you mix with 4 litres of water for sanitising?
quiz.explanation: 1 tablespoon of 5% bleach per 4 litres is the correct concentration for sanitising.

quiz.q: How often should you clean and sanitise work surfaces during continuous production?
options: D) Only at the end of the day
quiz.explanation: Every 4 hours prevents bacterial build-up during long production runs.

quiz.q: What should you do if you switch from raw tomatoes to finished sauce on the same surface?
options: A) Just wipe with a cloth
B) Clean and sanitise in between
C) Use the same surface without cleaning
quiz.explanation: Cleaning and sanitising prevents cross-contamination between raw and finished products.

quiz.q: What type of water should be used for washing tomatoes and making sauce?
quiz.explanation: Only potable water is safe to avoid introducing pathogens.

quiz.q: How can you treat water if you suspect it is contaminated?
quiz.explanation: Boiling for 1 minute kills most harmful bacteria and viruses.

quiz.q: What is the three-basin method used for?
quiz.explanation: Three basins (rinse, soap, final rinse) help wash tomatoes when water is scarce.

quiz.q: Why should you not let wastewater pool near the processing area?
options: B) It breeds mosquitoes and bacteria
quiz.explanation: Stagnant water is a breeding ground for pests and pathogens.

quiz.q: What is the maximum size of holes in screens to keep pests out?
quiz.explanation: 6 mm mesh prevents entry of most insects and rodents.

quiz.q: Where should you store rat poison?
quiz.explanation: Poison must be kept away from food to avoid contamination.

quiz.q: What should you do with bird droppings on roofs?
quiz.explanation: Covering tanks prevents droppings from contaminating water.

quiz.q: How should raw tomatoes be stored?
options: B) In clean crates off the floor
quiz.explanation: Off-floor storage prevents contamination from dirt and pests.

quiz.q: What is the ideal storage temperature for raw tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: 10â15Â°C slows ripening and spoilage without chilling injury.

quiz.q: What does FIFO stand for?
quiz.explanation: FIFO ensures older stock is used first to reduce spoilage.

quiz.q: How high should stored products be kept off the floor?
quiz.explanation: 15 cm off the floor prevents moisture and pest access.

quiz.q: Which bacterium is commonly associated with contaminated water?
quiz.explanation: E. coli is often waterborne and can cause severe illness.

quiz.q: What temperature should sauce be pasteurised to?
quiz.explanation: 85Â°C for 15 minutes kills most pathogens in sauce.

quiz.q: What pH level should tomato sauce be to prevent bacterial growth?
quiz.explanation: Acidic environment (pH < 4.6) inhibits harmful bacteria.

quiz.q: What is the danger zone for bacterial growth?
quiz.explanation: Bacteria multiply rapidly between 5Â°C and 60Â°C.

quiz.q: What should you do if a customer complains of illness after eating your product?
options: B) Investigate and recall if needed
quiz.explanation: Investigating and recalling protects public health and your reputation.

quiz.q: Why is mould on tomato sauce dangerous?
quiz.explanation: Mycotoxins can cause illness even if mould is removed.

quiz.q: What should you do before starting work if you have a cut on your hand?
quiz.explanation: Covering cuts prevents bacteria from entering food.

quiz.q: How often should you change your apron?
quiz.explanation: Daily or when dirty keeps contamination low.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to cough or sneeze in the processing area?
options: D) Turn away and cover with elbow
quiz.explanation: Turning away and using elbow prevents droplets from contaminating food.

quiz.q: What should you do with cleaning tools after use?
options: B) Store clean and off floor
quiz.explanation: Clean, off-floor storage prevents recontamination.

quiz.q: Why should you not store finished sauce in containers that held raw tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: Raw tomato residue can contain pathogens that contaminate finished sauce.

quiz.q: What is the best way to prevent pests from entering your processing area?
options: B) Seal cracks and use screens
quiz.explanation: Sealing cracks and screening openings blocks pest entry.
